text: Chilli crop guide Planting: Use healthy seedlings and plant in well-drained soil with good sunlight. Leave enough spacing for air movement. Water: Water when the topsoil begins to dry. Avoid waterlogging and wet leaves for long periods. Fertilizer: Add mature compost before planting. Apply fertilizer in small split doses during vegetative growth and flowering. Pests: Check leaves regularly for aphids, thrips, and mites. Remove badly affected plant parts and use locally approved control methods when needed. Diseases: Good drainage, clean tools, crop rotation, and removal of infected leaves help reduce disease spread. Harvest: Pick mature green or red chillies carefully to avoid damaging branches.

PADDY FIELD MACHINERY KNOWLEDGE BASE Purpose This knowledge base provides practical information about machines commonly used in paddy (rice) cultivation. It explains what each machine is used for, basic operating steps, suitable use cases, and important safety precautions. IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE Machine operation should always follow the manufacturer’s manual and the machine’s safety labels. Farmers should receive proper training before operating powered machinery. Never bypass guards or safety switches. Stop the engine, isolate the power source, and wait for moving parts to stop before clearing blockages, adjusting attachments, or performing maintenance. 1. Common paddy uses: - Pulling a mouldboard/disc plough. - Pulling a rotavator. - Pulling a puddler. - Pulling a harrow. - Operating a trailer. - Operating a compatible land-leveling implement. Attach the plough to the tractor’s three-point linkage. 2. Adjust working depth according to soil condition. 3. Start with a shallow test pass. 4. Adjust the implement for consistent soil turning. 5. Safety cautions: - Never stand behind or beside a suspended implement during attachment. - Lower the implement before inspection. - Do not make adjustments while the tractor or implement is moving. - Keep people away from the operating area. 4. GENERAL MACHINE SAFETY FOR PADDY FARMERS Before operating: - Read the operator manual. - Check fuel, oil, coolant, tyres, belts, chains, guards, brakes, steering, and hydraulic systems. - Check that all safety guards are installed. - Inspect the field for people, animals, large stones, deep holes, drains, and other obstacles. - Wear suitable footwear and clothing. - Use the required PPE. During operation: - Operate only machines you are trained to use. - Keep children and bystanders away. - Never wear loose clothing around rotating machinery. - Never put hands into moving mechanisms. - Do not exceed the machine’s rated capacity. - Maintain a safe speed. - Watch field edges, bunds, drains, slopes, and muddy areas. - Stop immediately if an unusual noise, vibration, smell, leak, or overheating condition occurs. AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: AI Safety The research agent should: - Prefer evidence-based management over unsupported claims. - State uncertainty when symptoms overlap. - Never claim that a virus-infected plant can be cured when the disease is not curable. - Avoid fixed fertilizer or pesticide doses without required field/product information. - Recommend local agricultural authorities for product registration and exact application instructions. - Prefer IPM and non-chemical controls before chemical intervention. - Distinguish prevention, treatment/management, and recovery. - Explain that damaged tissue may not recover even when the disease/pest is controlled.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Disease Disease: Bacterial Blight Scientific cause: Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae Identification / symptoms: - Water-soaked to yellowish lesions commonly begin near leaf margins or tips. - Lesions enlarge and may become pale yellow to whitish. - Severely affected leaves dry from the tip downward. - Young plants can wilt severely. - The disease is favored by stormy weather, strong winds, high humidity, and excessive nitrogen. Effects: - Reduces healthy leaf area and photosynthesis. - Severe infection can reduce grain filling and yield. Management: 1. Use resistant or locally recommended varieties where available. 2. Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer. 3. Maintain balanced plant nutrition. 4. Keep fields and irrigation channels clean and manage volunteer rice. 5. Avoid practices that unnecessarily injure plants. 6. Monitor fields regularly, especially after storms and during humid conditions. 7. Seek local extension advice before applying bactericides because chemical control can be limited and product registration varies by country. Recovery: - Remove or manage heavily infected plants when practical. - Maintain balanced nutrition and appropriate water management. - Protect remaining healthy plants

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Disease Disease: Blast Scientific cause: Magnaporthe oryzae Identification / symptoms: - Leaf lesions are often spindle- or diamond-shaped with pointed ends. - Lesions can enlarge and join together. - Collar or neck infections can cause serious damage to panicles. - Blast can be confused with brown spot, so diagnosis should consider lesion shape and plant stage. Effects: - Severe leaf blast can reduce leaf area available for grain filling. - Neck or panicle blast can cause poor grain development and major yield loss. Management: 1. Plant resistant varieties recommended for the local area. 2. Avoid excessive nitrogen. 3. Split nitrogen applications instead of applying excessive nitrogen at once. 4. Maintain suitable water management. 5. Use balanced nutrition. 6. Use clean seed and good field sanitation. 7. Where locally recommended and legally registered, fungicides such as appropriate triazole or strobilurin products may be used according to the label and local extension guidance. 8. Monitor especially around heading when neck blast risk is important. Recovery: - Existing dead lesions will not become healthy again. - Protect

Recovery: - Existing dead lesions will not become healthy again. - Protect newly emerging leaves and panicles. - Correct excessive nitrogen or other management problems. - Severe neck blast should be reported to an agricultural officer because yield protection may require timely intervention.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Disease Disease: Brown Spot Scientific cause: Bipolaris oryzae (commonly associated with brown spot) Identification / symptoms: - Small circular to oval brown lesions occur on leaves. - Mature lesions may have a darker margin and lighter center. - Severe infection can affect grains. - Brown spot can be confused with blast. Common contributing factors: - Nutrient stress, particularly poor overall crop nutrition. - Drought or water stress. - Poor soil fertility. - Weak or stressed plants. Effects: - Reduced photosynthesis. - Reduced grain quality and yield under severe disease pressure. Management: 1. Maintain balanced soil fertility. 2. Correct confirmed nutrient deficiencies. 3. Avoid prolonged water stress. 4. Use healthy seed. 5. Remove or manage infected crop residues where appropriate. 6. Improve field sanitation. 7. Use locally recommended fungicide options only when needed and according to local labels. Recovery: - Correct underlying nutrient or water stress. - Protect new growth. - Severely damaged leaves will not recover, but improved management can reduce new infection.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Disease Disease: Tungro Cause: - Rice tungro disease is caused by a combination of rice tungro viruses. - Green leafhoppers are important vectors. Identification / symptoms: - Yellow to orange-yellow leaves. - Stunted plants. - Reduced tillering. - Symptoms can resemble nitrogen deficiency, zinc deficiency, water stress, or pest damage. Effects: - Severe early infection can strongly reduce plant growth and yield. Important fact: - An already infected rice plant cannot be cured of tungro. Management: 1. Plant tungro- or leafhopper-resistant varieties where locally available. 2. Synchronize planting with neighboring farms when practical. 3. Avoid planting at times of high green leafhopper abundance where local guidance supports this. 4. Remove severely infected plants when appropriate. 5. Plow infected stubble after harvest according to local recommendations. 6. Manage weeds and volunteer rice that may support vectors. 7. Do not rely on insecticide alone because green leafhoppers can move rapidly between fields. Recovery: - Individual infected plants cannot be cured. - Protect the rest of the crop by reducing vector pressure and removing infection sources. -

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: General Recovery When a farmer asks “How can I recover my rice crop?”: 1. Identify the likely problem first. 2. Check crop age and growth stage. 3. Inspect several plants rather than one plant. 4. Look for patterns across the field. 5. Check recent fertilizer use and water management. 6. Check for insects, disease lesions, and nutrient symptoms. 7. Correct the underlying cause. 8. Protect healthy/new growth. 9. Avoid unnecessary pesticide applications. 10. Use resistant varieties and good field sanitation for future crops. 11. If diagnosis is uncertain or damage is severe, recommend professional confirmation.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Nutrition Nutrition: Nitrogen (N) Deficiency Role: - Nitrogen is essential for vegetative growth, chlorophyll formation, and yield. Typical symptoms: - Older leaves become yellowish or pale green first. - Plants may be stunted. - Reduced tillering. - Overall crop growth is weak. Possible causes: - Low soil nitrogen. - Insufficient fertilizer. - Nutrient losses. - Poor timing or placement of nitrogen fertilizer. Management / recovery: 1. Confirm the diagnosis because yellowing can have several causes. 2. Follow a site-specific or locally recommended nitrogen management plan. 3. Apply nitrogen at the recommended rate and timing rather than applying a large amount at once. 4. Split nitrogen applications where recommended. 5. Consider soil and crop history. 6. Avoid over-application because excessive nitrogen can increase susceptibility to some pests and diseases. Warning: - Do not tell a farmer to apply a fixed amount of urea without knowing field size, soil condition, crop stage, previous fertilizer use, and local recommendation.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Nutrition Nutrition: Phosphorus (P) Deficiency Role: - Important for root development, energy transfer, early growth, and reproductive development. Typical symptoms: - Stunted growth. - Dark green foliage may occur. - Reduced tillering. - Delayed crop development. Management / recovery: 1. Confirm deficiency using soil/plant assessment where possible. 2. Apply phosphorus according to soil test and local rice fertilizer recommendations. 3. Correct soil conditions that reduce phosphorus availability when applicable. 4. Avoid unnecessary over-application.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Nutrition Nutrition: Potassium (K) Deficiency Role: - Supports water regulation, plant strength, stress tolerance, and disease/pest resilience. Possible symptoms: - Older leaves may develop yellowing or browning, especially toward margins or tips. - Weak growth and reduced stress tolerance can occur. - Symptoms vary with variety and soil conditions. Management / recovery: 1. Confirm potassium deficiency rather than diagnosing only from leaf color. 2. Apply potassium according to soil testing or locally recommended rice nutrient management. 3. Maintain balanced N-P-K nutrition. 4. Avoid excessive nitrogen without adequate potassium because nutrient imbalance can increase crop problems.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Pest Pest: Brown Planthopper (BPH) Common name: Brown planthopper Scientific group: Nilaparvata lugens Damage / symptoms: - Nymphs and adults suck plant sap. - Heavy infestation causes hopper burn: leaves dry and plants turn brown. - Plants may lodge. - BPH can transmit grassy stunt and ragged stunt viruses. Management: 1. Monitor fields regularly. 2. Use locally recommended resistant varieties where available. 3. Avoid excessive nitrogen. 4. Avoid unnecessary early-season insecticide applications. 5. Protect natural enemies such as spiders. 6. Drain or manage water according to local recommendations when BPH pressure is high. 7. If insecticide is justified by monitoring and threshold information, use a locally registered selective product according to its label. Recovery: - Reduce pest pressure quickly when economic thresholds are exceeded. - Allow surviving plants to recover through good water and nutrient management. - Severely hopper-burned plants may not recover fully.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Pest Pest: Green Leafhopper (GLH) Damage / symptoms: - Adults and nymphs suck sap from leaves. - Heavy feeding can weaken plants. - Important vector of tungro disease. Management: 1. Use resistant varieties where available. 2. Synchronize planting where practical. 3. Remove volunteer rice and manage weeds that can maintain vector populations. 4. Monitor populations. 5. Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural enemies. 6. Manage tungro by reducing vector movement and using resistant varieties. Recovery: - Reduce leafhopper pressure and protect young plants. - If tungro has already infected plants, the virus cannot be cured; protect the remaining crop.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Pest Pest: Rice Leaffolder Scientific group: Cnaphalocrocis medinalis and related species Damage / symptoms: - Larvae fold or roll leaves and feed inside the folded leaf. - White or transparent feeding areas may appear. - Severe damage reduces photosynthetic leaf area. Management: 1. Inspect folded leaves and larval presence. 2. Early damage is often tolerated by rice because plants can compensate. 3. Avoid routine insecticide spraying during early crop stages unless monitoring indicates a real need. 4. Preserve parasitoids, predators, and other natural enemies. 5. Use insecticide only when economically justified and locally recommended. Recovery: - Healthy rice can produce new leaves after moderate early damage. - Maintain good crop nutrition and water management.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Pest Pest: Rice Bug Common name: Rice bug / rice stink bug Damage / symptoms: - Adults and nymphs suck developing grains. - Damaged grains may become discolored, shriveled, or poorly filled. - Damage is particularly important around flowering and grain development. Management: 1. Monitor fields during flowering and grain filling. 2. Remove or manage weeds that provide alternate habitat when practical. 3. Maintain field sanitation. 4. Use locally recommended control only when monitoring indicates an economically important infestation. 5. Protect natural enemies. Recovery: - Damaged grains cannot be restored. - The goal is to protect remaining developing grains.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Pest Pest: Stem Borer Examples: - Yellow stem borer - Striped stem borer - Other rice stem borers Damage / symptoms: - Larvae bore into stems. - Vegetative-stage damage causes deadhearts. - Reproductive-stage damage can cause whiteheads. - Frass or larval material may be found inside damaged stems. Management: 1. Use resistant or locally suitable varieties. 2. Handpick and destroy egg masses where practical. 3. Synchronize planting. 4. Remove volunteer rice and manage crop residues. 5. Harvest and manage stubble appropriately. 6. Encourage natural enemies and biological control. 7. Apply nitrogen according to recommended timing and rate. 8. Use insecticide only when justified by monitoring and local recommendations. Recovery: - Dead tillers generally will not recover. - Protect unaffected tillers and panicles. - Improve field sanitation for the next crop.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Rice Category: Pest Pest: Whorl Maggot Scientific name commonly associated with rice whorl maggot: Hydrellia spp.; species vary by region. Damage / symptoms: - Maggots feed on young tissue inside the whorl. - Young leaves may show yellowish-white longitudinal damage. - Leaves may shrivel or show holes. - Severe damage can delay maturity. Management: 1. Early crop damage is often tolerated and rice may compensate. 2. Remove alternate hosts where practical. 3. Adjust planting time according to local recommendations. 4. Maintain balanced potassium and overall nutrient management. 5. Encourage natural enemies. 6. Avoid unnecessary early insecticide applications. Recovery: - New leaves can develop after early damage. - Severe or persistent damage should be assessed by an agricultural officer.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: AI Safety The research agent should: - Clearly distinguish diagnosis from suspicion. - Avoid saying that a viral disease can be cured when it cannot. - Avoid inventing pesticide names, rates, or application schedules. - Recommend label-compliant and locally registered products only. - Prefer IPM and cultural controls. - Explain uncertainty when symptoms overlap. - Avoid presenting a single symptom as proof of a disease. - Ask for crop stage, location, symptoms, photos, weather, irrigation, and fertilizer history when these details materially affect the recommendation. - Escalate uncertain or severe cases to agricultural professionals.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 1. BACTERIAL SPOT Scientific cause: Xanthomonas spp. (X. euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans). Identification / symptoms: - Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown to black with a yellow halo. - Spots may merge and cause leaf tearing or drop. - Raised, scabby, rough spots appear on green fruit. Effects: - Heavy leaf loss reduces plant vigor and sunscald risk on fruit. - Blemished fruit lowers market quality even when yield is not badly affected. Management: 1. Use certified disease-free seed and transplants. 2. Avoid overhead irrigation and working in wet foliage. 3. Rotate away from tomato and pepper for at least one season. 4. Apply copper-based bactericides preventively where locally approved. 5. Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest. Recovery: - Spotted leaves will not clear up; focus on protecting new growth. - Improve airflow and reduce leaf wetness duration. - Severe, spreading outbreaks should be confirmed by an extension officer.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 2. EARLY BLIGHT Scientific cause: Alternaria solani. Identification / symptoms: - Dark brown spots with concentric rings forming a target/bullseye pattern, usually on older, lower leaves first. - Yellow tissue often surrounds each spot. - Sunken, dark lesions can also appear on stems and near the fruit stem end. Effects: - Progressive loss of lower leaves reduces photosynthesis and can expose fruit to sunscald. - Stem lesions can weaken young plants. Management: 1. Rotate crops away from tomato and potato for 2-3 years. 2. Mulch to reduce soil splash onto leaves. 3. Remove infected lower leaves promptly. 4. Ensure adequate plant spacing for airflow. 5. Apply labelled fungicides such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb where locally approved once symptoms appear. Recovery: - Existing lesions do not heal, so protect healthy new foliage. - Correct crowding, mulch coverage, and irrigation practices that keep leaves wet.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 3. HEALTHY TOMATO Identification: - Leaves are uniformly green with no spots, mold, curling, mottling, or wilting. - No visible pest damage, webbing, or scabby lesions on fruit or stems. - Growth is even and vigorous for the plant's stage. Notes: - This class is the baseline reference used to confirm that a plant shows no signs of the diseases or pests covered in this knowledge base. - A healthy classification does not rule out early-stage or symptomless problems, so continue routine monitoring of leaf undersides and new growth. Recommended care: 1. Maintain consistent watering and avoid prolonged leaf wetness. 2. Keep balanced fertilization based on plant stage. 3. Continue regular visual inspection, especially after wet or humid weather.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 4. LATE BLIGHT Scientific cause: Phytophthora infestans. Identification / symptoms: - Irregular, dark, water-soaked, greasy-looking lesions on leaves, often starting at leaf edges or tips. - A pale green-to-yellow halo may surround lesions. - White, fuzzy fungal growth can appear on the underside of leaves in humid conditions. - Dark, firm, greasy blotches can develop on fruit. Effects: - One of the most destructive tomato diseases; it can defoliate and kill plants within days under cool, wet, humid conditions. - Infected fruit is unmarketable and infection can continue to spread after harvest. Management: 1. Act quickly at first sign of symptoms; this disease spreads fast. 2. Remove and destroy infected plants or plant parts away from the field. 3. Avoid overhead irrigation and working in wet foliage. 4. Apply labelled protectant fungicides (e.g. chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper products) where locally approved, especially before forecast cool wet weather. 5. Use resistant or tolerant varieties where available. Recovery: - Badly affected plants rarely recover; prioritize protecting unaffected plants and neighboring fields. - Report widespread or

forecast cool wet weather. 5. Use resistant or tolerant varieties where available. Recovery: - Badly affected plants rarely recover; prioritize protecting unaffected plants and neighboring fields. - Report widespread or rapidly spreading outbreaks to an agricultural extension officer.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 5. LEAF MOLD Scientific cause: Passalora fulva (syn. Fulvia fulva / Cladosporium fulvum). Identification / symptoms: - Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface. - Olive-green to grayish-purple velvety mold growth on the corresponding underside of the leaf. - Most common in greenhouses or areas with high humidity and poor air circulation. Effects: - Reduced photosynthesis from leaf yellowing and early leaf drop, which can lower yield in enclosed or densely planted conditions. Management: 1. Improve ventilation and reduce humidity around plants. 2. Increase plant spacing and prune for better airflow. 3. Avoid overhead watering, especially late in the day. 4. Use resistant varieties where available. 5. Apply labelled fungicides if the disease is severe or persistent. Recovery: - Improving airflow and humidity control usually stops further spread. - Remove heavily affected leaves to reduce spore load.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 6. SEPTORIA LEAF SPOT Scientific cause: Septoria lycopersici. Identification / symptoms: - Small, circular spots with dark brown margins and light gray or tan centers, usually starting on older, lower leaves. - Tiny black specks (pycnidia) are often visible in the center of spots. - Spots can be numerous and merge, causing yellowing and leaf drop. Effects: - Progressive lower-leaf loss reduces plant vigor and can expose fruit to sunscald if defoliation is severe. Management: 1. Remove and destroy infected lower leaves as symptoms appear. 2. Mulch around plants to reduce soil splash. 3. Rotate crops away from tomato for at least one season. 4. Avoid overhead irrigation and working with wet foliage. 5. Apply labelled fungicides where locally approved for persistent outbreaks. Recovery: - Existing spots will not clear; protect new upper growth by controlling humidity and leaf wetness.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 8. TARGET SPOT Scientific cause: Corynespora cassiicola. Identification / symptoms: - Brown lesions with faint concentric rings, similar to early blight but often larger and less defined. - Spots can appear on leaves, stems, and fruit. - Lesions may have a slightly sunken center and can merge to form large necrotic patches. Effects: - Significant leaf loss under warm, humid conditions can reduce yield and expose fruit to sun damage. - Fruit lesions reduce marketability. Management: 1. Rotate crops and avoid continuous tomato planting. 2. Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest. 3. Improve airflow through spacing and pruning. 4. Avoid prolonged leaf wetness from overhead irrigation. 5. Apply labelled fungicides in rotation where the disease is severe or persistent. Recovery: - Focus on protecting healthy foliage; existing lesions will not heal. - Reduce humidity and leaf wetness where practical.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 9. TOMATO MOSAIC VIRUS Scientific cause: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV). Identification / symptoms: - Light and dark green mottled (mosaic) pattern on leaves. - Leaf distortion, curling, or fern-like narrowing in severe cases. - Stunted growth and reduced fruit set or quality. Effects: - No direct cure exists; yield and fruit quality losses depend on infection timing and severity. - The virus is very stable and can persist in plant debris, soil, and on tools or hands for a long time. Management: 1. Remove and destroy infected plants; there is no chemical cure. 2. Disinfect tools and wash hands between handling plants, especially after contact with tobacco products, which can carry the virus. 3. Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties where available. 4. Avoid working in the crop when plants are wet. Recovery: - Infected plants do not recover; focus on preventing spread to healthy plants. - Practice strict sanitation for future plantings.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Disease 10. TOMATO YELLOW LEAF CURL VIRUS (TYLCV) Scientific cause: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. Identification / symptoms: - Upward curling and yellowing of leaflet margins. - Stunted, bushy growth with small, pale leaves. - Flower drop and greatly reduced fruit set on infected plants. Effects: - Yield loss can be severe, especially when plants are infected young. - The virus spreads rapidly wherever whitefly populations are high. Management: 1. Control whitefly populations using recommended insecticides or biological controls. 2. Use resistant or tolerant varieties where available. 3. Remove and destroy infected plants early to reduce virus source. 4. Use reflective mulches or fine exclusion netting to deter whiteflies. 5. Avoid planting new seedlings next to heavily infected fields. Recovery: - Infected plants do not recover; prevention through whitefly control is the main defense. - Monitor new growth closely after transplanting.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: General Recovery When a farmer asks how to recover a tomato plant: 1. Identify the likely disease/pest first. 2. Check whether the problem is fungal, bacterial, viral, insect-related, or environmental. 3. Inspect multiple leaves and plants. 4. Check the underside of leaves for mites and insects. 5. Check irrigation, humidity, drainage, temperature, and recent weather. 6. Review fertilizer use and nutrient balance. 7. Remove or isolate severely infected plant material when appropriate. 8. Improve airflow and reduce unnecessary leaf wetness. 9. Use resistant varieties for future planting where available. 10. Use chemical control only when justified and according to local label requirements. 11. For suspected viral disease, focus on prevention and vector management rather than attempting a “cure”. 12. If diagnosis is uncertain or the crop is severely affected, recommend confirmation by an agricultural extension officer or plant pathologist.

AgriKetha-AI Knowledge Base Crop: Tomato Category: Pest 7. SPIDER MITES (TWO-SPOTTED SPIDER MITE) Scientific cause: Tetranychus urticae. Identification / symptoms: - Fine yellow or white stippling/speckling on leaves, often starting on the underside. - Leaves can turn bronze or yellow and dry out under heavy infestation. - Fine webbing may be visible on the underside of leaves or between stems in severe cases. - Mites are tiny and often easier to detect with a hand lens than with the naked eye. Effects: - Reduced photosynthesis and leaf drop under heavy infestation, lowering yield and plant vigor. - Populations build up fastest in hot, dry, dusty conditions. Management: 1. Increase humidity and reduce plant dust where practical. 2. Use insecticidal soap or labelled miticides for heavy infestations. 3. Encourage natural predators such as predatory mites. 4. Remove heavily infested leaves. 5. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural mite predators. Recovery: - Damaged leaves will not regreen; focus on stopping further spread and protecting new growth. - Recheck leaf undersides regularly after treatment.
